title: Arithmetic progressions of Gaussian primes
statement: A Gaussian prime is a prime element of Z[i]: a + bi with a^2 + b^2 a prime (a, b nonzero), or an associate of a prime p = 3 (mod 4). A k-term progression is a, a + d, ..., a + (k - 1)d with d a nonzero Gaussian integer; Tao (2006) proved that the Gaussian primes contain progressions (and constellations of every shape) of every length. Let M(k) be the least possible largest norm of a k-term progression of Gaussian primes. We find M(k) exactly for k <= 18 (table). The headline cell asks for the longest progression of Gaussian primes all of whose norms are at most 10^11: the best known has 18 terms (ours, all norms at most 557,124,937).
submission: Text file: one line 'x y' per term x + yi of the progression, in order; every term a Gaussian prime of norm at most 10^11.
score: the number of terms, an integer (larger is better)

best_known.source: Quantavane (Arhan Canli), 9 November 2026: exhaustive search over common differences d in 1105(1 + i)Z[i] and all first terms with bit tables of the Gaussian primes of norm up to 1.2 x 10^9 (tools/src/gaussap.c, mode big)

context: Green and Tao proved that the primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, and Tao (2006) that the Gaussian primes contain every finite constellation; both proofs are existence proofs. For the rational primes the least progressions of each length are tabulated and the longest known has 27 terms (PrimeGrid, 2019). For the Gaussian primes we found no computation of explicit long progressions. The arithmetic of Z[i] shapes them: if k >= 10 the common difference must be divisible by 5(1 + i), because otherwise two terms would be divisible by 2 + i (or by 1 + i) and both would have to be the same small prime; a prime ideal P of norm k or less either divides d or contains one term of norm N(P). Inert primes such as 3 and 7 never force anything, since the progression meets only p of the p^2 residue classes modulo p. These facts reduce each length to a few exhaustive searches: M(k) is known exactly for k <= 18 here, and it jumps irregularly (M(12) = 122,033, M(13) = 7,114,409, M(14) = 8,565,209). The least 17-term progression extends to 18 terms with the same largest norm, and no 19-term progression has d in 1105(1 + i)Z[i] and norms up to 1.4 x 10^9. How long a progression fits under 10^11, and how M(k) grows, are open.
references: T. Tao, The Gaussian primes contain arbitrarily shaped constellations, J. Anal. Math. 99 (2006) 109-176 (arXiv:math/0501314)
B. Green, T. Tao, The primes contain arbitrarily long arithmetic progressions, Ann. of Math. 167 (2008) 481-547
E. Gethner, S. Wagon, B. Wick, A stroll through the Gaussian primes, Amer. Math. Monthly 105 (1998) 327-337
J. K. Andersen, Primes in arithmetic progression records (web page)

novelty.verdict: new question: long progressions in the Gaussian primes are known to exist (Tao 2006); no computation of explicit progressions, of least norms or of the longest progression in a disc was found.
closest: T. Tao (2006): existence of every constellation in the Gaussian primes, with no explicit examples or bounds usable for computation.
Records for rational primes (minimal and longest progressions, PrimeGrid and others): the same questions in Z.
Our problem gauss-admissible: admissible constellations (no primality) of smallest diameter in Z[i].
novelty.benchmark: no prime-progression family in the benchmark

first_values.note: Exact values from tools/src/gaussap.c: mode exact (every pair of terms) for k <= 11; for larger k the necessary divisibility of d and the case split by small prime ideals (modes fast, big and through), each search complete up to a norm bound above the value found.
